name: TP4056-42-ESOP8
title: TP4056: 1 A standalone linear charger for one Li-ion cell, 4.2 V
summary: A linear CC/CV charger for a single lithium-ion cell, with the pass transistor and current sensing on chip, so one resistor on PROG sets a charge current of up to 1000 mA. The float voltage is fixed at 4.2 V ±1%; deeply discharged cells are trickle-charged below 2.9 V, charging ends at one tenth of the set current, and the cell is recharged automatically when it sags below about 4.05 V. It has two open-drain status outputs, a thermistor input that pauses charging outside a temperature window, undervoltage lockout, die-temperature regulation and a chip-enable pin. It comes in ESOP8 and EMSOP8 packages.

pins.name: TEMP
pins.function: Battery temperature sense input, taken from the NTC thermistor divider of the pack. Charging is held off while its voltage is under 45% or over 80% of the supply. Grounding TEMP turns the temperature check off.

pins.name: PROG
pins.function: Charge current set and monitor. A resistor RPROG to GND sets the charge current. The pin sits at 1 V in constant-current mode and at 0.1 V in recharge mode; in any charging mode IBAT = (VPROG/RPROG) × 1100. Left open, the charger shuts down.

pins.name: VCC
pins.function: Supply input that powers the charger. When VCC comes within 30 mV of the BAT voltage the part shuts down and BAT draws under 2 µA.

pins.name: BAT
pins.function: Battery connection, to the cell's positive terminal. Delivers the charge current and holds the final float voltage at 4.2 V. Draws under 2 µA in sleep or with the chip disabled.

pins.name: STDBY
pins.function: Charge-complete status, active low. Driven low once a charge cycle ends; high impedance otherwise.

pins.name: CHRG
pins.function: Charging status, active low. Pulled low while the battery is charging; high impedance otherwise.

pins.name: CE
pins.function: Chip enable. High runs the charger normally; low puts it in shutdown. Accepts TTL or CMOS levels.

pins.name: exposed pad
pins.function: Metal pad on the underside of the package; solder it to PCB ground for full charge current.

circuits.title: Charger with battery temperature sensing and two status LEDs
circuits.description: A 5 V supply feeds VCC and CE together, so the charger is always enabled. RPROG on PROG sets the charge current. Two LEDs with 1 kΩ resistors sit on the open-drain status outputs: the red one on CHRG lights while charging, the green one on STDBY lights when charging is done. R1 from VCC and R2 to ground, with the pack's NTC thermistor across R2, set the voltage on TEMP so that charging pauses when the cell is too hot or too cold. 10 µF capacitors decouple VCC and BAT.

circuits.title: Charger with one charging LED, no temperature sensing
circuits.description: VCC and CE are tied to the 5 V supply. One LED with a 1 kΩ resistor on CHRG shows charging. STDBY and TEMP go to ground, which turns the temperature check off. RPROG sets the charge current; 10 µF capacitors decouple VCC and BAT.

circuits.title: Charger with no status LEDs and no temperature sensing
circuits.description: The smallest arrangement: VCC and CE on the 5 V supply, CHRG, STDBY and TEMP grounded, RPROG to set the current, and 10 µF on VCC and on BAT.

circuits.title: USB and wall adapter inputs (simple)
circuits.description: Two supplies share VCC. The wall adapter reaches VCC through Schottky diode D1. USB reaches VCC through P-channel MOSFET M1, whose gate sits on the wall adapter line with a 10 kΩ pull-down: with no adapter the gate is held low and M1 conducts; with the adapter present the gate is high and M1 is off, so USB is cut off.
notes: U1's other pins are not part of this circuit.

circuits.title: Red and green status LEDs with a series input resistor for heat
circuits.description: The supply reaches VCC through a 0.4 Ω resistor, which takes part of the dropped voltage and so part of the heat off the chip. VCC and CE are tied together. A red LED on CHRG (charging) and a green LED on STDBY (done), each with 1 kΩ, show status. TEMP is grounded, RPROG sets the current, 10 µF decouples VCC and BAT.

circuits.title: PROG pin isolated from a capacitive load and filtered
circuits.description: To read the average charge current, a 10 kΩ resistor runs from PROG to a filter capacitor, and the monitoring circuit reads the capacitor. The resistor keeps the filter capacitance off the PROG node so the current loop stays stable.
notes: U1's other pins are not part of this circuit.

circuits.title: Series input resistor to raise the charge current under thermal limit
circuits.description: The supply VS reaches VCC through RCC, with 1 µF from VCC to ground. RCC drops part of the excess voltage outside the chip, so less power is spent inside it and the thermal loop allows more charge current.

circuits.title: Reverse input polarity protection with a P-channel MOSFET
circuits.description: A P-channel MOSFET sits in series between VIN and VCC with its gate grounded. With the right polarity it turns on and passes the supply with little drop; with VIN reversed it stays off and its body diode blocks.

parts.note: its drain-bulk diode points from VIN toward VCC

notes: U1's other pins are not part of this circuit.

circuits.title: USB and wall adapter power with charge current switched by source
circuits.description: The wall adapter (600 mA) feeds VCC through Schottky D1; USB (500 mA) feeds VCC through P-channel MP1, whose gate is on the wall adapter line. The same line drives the gate of N-channel MN1, held low by 10 kΩ when no adapter is present. PROG has 2 kΩ to ground at all times; when the adapter is present MN1 turns on and adds 10 kΩ in parallel, raising the charge current. BAT feeds the cell and the system load.
notes: U1's GND, CE, TEMP, CHRG and STDBY are not part of this circuit.

operation.text: A linear charger, constant current then constant voltage, for one lithium-ion cell, delivering up to 1 A with the float voltage held to ±1%. The pass device is an internal PMOS, so the cell needs neither a blocking diode nor a current-sense resistor, and the battery cannot discharge back through it. Two open-drain pins report state: CHRG while charging, STDBY when done.

Charging starts once VCC is above the UVLO threshold, a resistor is on PROG and CE is high. While BAT is below the trickle threshold (2.9 V typical, 2.8 to 3.0 V) the part charges at a tenth of the programmed current; above it, it charges at the full programmed current. Near 4.2 V the current tapers as the part regulates voltage, and when it falls to one tenth of the programmed value the cycle ends: CHRG releases and STDBY pulls low.

End of charge is detected on PROG: when its voltage stays under 100 mV for longer than the filter time (1.8 ms typical) charging stops and stays off, and the part sits in standby, with supply current near 55 µA. The filter keeps short load transients on BAT from ending the cycle early. C/10 termination is inactive during trickle charging and thermal limiting. After termination the battery alone supplies any load on BAT.

In standby the part watches BAT. If it falls below the 4.05 V recharge threshold (roughly 80 to 90% of capacity) for longer than the 1.8 ms filter, a new cycle starts and CHRG pulls low again. The return from standby to charging is also given as VBAT < 4.12 V.

With no input, or with the input below VBAT, the part sleeps and battery drain falls to under 3 µA (−2 µA max at VCC = 0 V). Pulling CE low or leaving PROG open shuts the charger down at any time: battery drain under 2 µA, supply current under 55 µA. Raising CE or reconnecting RPROG restarts it.

The charger stays in shutdown while VCC is below the UVLO threshold (3.7 V typical; 3.6 V is also given) or below VBAT, and after a trip it stays off until VCC is 100 mV above the battery. In lockout both CHRG and STDBY are high impedance.

An internal loop reduces the charge current when the die tries to exceed a set point of about 140 to 145°C, and cuts it to zero above 150°C. Charge current can therefore be chosen for typical ambient conditions and the part protects itself in worst-case ones.

TEMP is compared with 45% and 80% of VCC. Outside that window the cell is taken to be too hot or too cold and charging is suspended; it resumes once TEMP returns inside it. Because both thresholds are fractions of VCC, the temperature window depends only on R1, R2 and the thermistor, not on the supply. Grounding TEMP turns the check off.

CHRG pulls low throughout a charge cycle, recharges included, and is high impedance otherwise. STDBY pulls low when charging is complete. Both are high impedance when the cell temperature is out of range or the input is in lockout. With TEMP grounded and no battery but 10 µF on BAT, CHRG blinks with a period of 1 to 4 s. Unused status pins are tied to GND.
At the start of each charge cycle the current ramps from zero to full over about 20 µs, limiting inrush on the supply.

Multilayer ceramic input capacitors can ring and produce high voltage spikes when the charger is plugged into a live supply, because of their high Q. A 1.5 Ω resistor in series with the ceramic capacitor keeps these start-up transients down.

operation.topic: Increasing charge current with a series resistor
operation.text: A resistor between the supply and VCC moves part of the dissipation off the chip, so more current is available before thermal limiting. With VS 5 V, 800 mA programmed, VBAT 3.75 V and θJA 125°C/W the reachable current rises from 768 mA to 948 mA. If VCC falls far enough that the charger enters dropout, charging slows, so RCC has to be small enough to avoid that.
Where the input may be reversed, a series blocking diode suits a high supply voltage; a P-channel MOSFET suits a low-drop design.

Where average rather than peak battery current matters, for instance with a switching load on the battery, an RC filter on PROG gives it. A 10 kΩ resistor between PROG and the filter capacitor keeps the loop stable.

Place RPROG close to the chip and keep stray capacitance on PROG small. Put the VCC and BAT capacitors close to the chip. Heat leaves through the leads, mainly the ground lead, and the exposed pad into board copper, so pads should be wide and run out to large copper areas, with vias to inner or back layers; the exposed pad must be soldered to ground for full current. Other heat sources on the board add to the temperature rise.
